source_title: Local know-how helps communities make the most of new technology and opportunities - Microsoft Source
source_excerpt:
New technology is creating new opportunities for people to learn and build skills.
Local organizations are responding based on the people they serve, from building digital confidence to preparing people for work.
Microsoft is supporting those efforts through investments in local nonprofits, AI skills and training.
In Virginia’s rural Mecklenburg County, residents often go to the library for help with tasks many people take for granted. Staff show patrons how to get online, open and print documents or send emails from their phones. Many don’t have computers at home; others borrow DVDs because they lack internet service to stream movies.
But in recent months, some are showing up at their local branches eager to learn about AI. Connie Boyd, the branch manager for the library in Clarksville, says she and her colleagues are learning about it themselves as they begin offering classes to help residents explore a technology that’s increasingly changing how people work, learn and find information.
“A computer opens doors,” Boyd says, “and AI will open a door for them.”
The classes are supported by Microsoft as part of a new program designed in collaboration with the Public Library Association — just one way the company is investing in communities to help residents access new skills, training and opportunities. Locals play a central role in shaping these efforts, whether they’re librarians, workforce counselors, nonprofit leaders or others who know their neighbors and what they might need.
Robert Rosenthal, the county library director, realized earlier this year that staff and patrons alike were encountering AI without necessarily understanding what it was or what they might use it for. The county of about 30,000 has lost traditional industries over the years even as new datacenters and associated jobs have arrived, and Rosenthal saw an opportunity to help residents become “a little more comfortable and a little less fearful” of technology.
With training and staff support from Microsoft, the library system launched the program as a pilot a few months ago to help residents build confidence using AI and understand how it could support their daily lives.
Eighteen people showed up at Boyd’s first AI class in August, almost triple the turnout for classes she’d organized on other subjects in her town of about 1,300 people. They ranged from young adults to retirees, and she says most came because they didn’t know what AI was and were curious. Some were surprised to discover they were already using it when they spoke into their phones or saw generated answers in search results.
For Boyd, who started working at one of the county’s four libraries in 2004, the class was an extension of what libraries already do: give people a trusted place to learn, ask questions, find information and become comfortable using tools themselves.
The library support is part of Microsoft’s Community-First AI Infrastructure commitment to the communities around its datacenters.
Microsoft’s Community-First AI Infrastructure initiative is a set of commitments to the places where it builds and operates datacenters. The idea is that communities hosting the infrastructure needed for AI should share its benefits without having to shoulder added costs.
The plan has five parts: Microsoft says it will pay its share of electricity costs so they aren’t passed on to residents; reduce its water use and replenish more water than it uses; create local jobs; contribute to the tax base that supports hospitals, schools, parks and libraries; and invest in local AI training and nonprofits.
“Every community is unique, and lasting progress starts with listening to the people who know it best,” says Justin Spelhaug, president of Microsoft Elevate , which leads the company’s nonprofit, education and workforce programs. “Local schools, libraries, nonprofits and small businesses are trusted voices with deep insight into what their neighbors need. Microsoft can bring technology, resources and support, but working alongside these organizations is how we turn those tools into meaningful opportunities for people.”
At a workforce nonprofit in Wyoming, the most valuable technology may be the kind its clients never see.
Single moms often arrive at Climb Wyoming navigating poverty, childcare and housing while grieving a death or divorce, recovering from trauma or rebuilding after incarceration. Experiences like those can make it hard to plan, prioritize or regulate emotions, says Molly Kruger, the organization’s chief operating officer.
So Climb Wyoming tries to provide a healing environment that feels safe and predictable, Kruger says.
Its six locations across the state are designed to feel safe and welcoming, with couches, lamps, photographs of graduates and calendars on the walls. Staff greet women with thoughtful phrases like “I’m so glad you’re here; I bet it took a lot to get here,” before diving into their backgrounds and needs. Details like that, along with a predictable program structure, are intended to reduce anxiety and help participants regain a sense of control as they take work- and life-skills classes and move toward job placement.
At the Cheyenne location, 94% of participants have graduated over the past five years, and graduates’ average monthly wages rose to about $2,900 from about $1,600 before the program.
But providing individualized support requires time. Kruger has been thinking about that more since becoming a fellow of Microsoft’s TechSpark program , which trains nonprofit leaders to expand local technology programs and provides grants to support AI projects.
Microsoft created TechSpark to work with local organizations on expanding access to technology, digital skills and economic opportunities. Rather than bringing the same program to every place, it works with people and organizations already rooted there to identify local needs and develop programs around them.
Through the TechSpark Fellows program, participating nonprofits select a leader who receives training, coaching and connections to a national network of peers. Fellows use what they learn to develop or expand technology and AI programs within their organizations and the communities they serve. The fellowship typically lasts two years, with participants able to stay connected afterward through an alumni network.
The new connections with other nonprofits around the country inspired Kruger to begin looking at whether technology could take some of the administrative work off employees’ plates so they’d have more time to spend with clients.
Climb Wyoming, which just celebrated its 40 th anniversary, digitized mental health assessments and other paperwork and is using AI tools to create automated reports that help staff see more quickly where best to focus their efforts during the short 12-week programs.
“The more we can spend with families that we’re working with and less on burdensome tasks, the better,” Kruger says, adding that AI “has been a helpful thinking partner.”
The organization also has used AI to help preserve its specific communication style in training materials and evolving policies, including in its employee handbook, and help with data analysis to become more effective and efficient.
“We have a certain tone that is important to us that’s really caring but also very direct,” Kruger says. “We really want to have this psychologically informed environment.”
Not only that, but “tech is woven across industries,” so her TechSpark experience is helping her think about how the jobs Climb Wyoming’s participants are preparing for are changing, and how trainers can incorporate AI skills into the coursework.
For many families, the barrier to participating in a digital economy is more basic: They need a reliable computer, internet access and the skills to use them.
Compudopt is a Houston-based nonprofit most known for refurbishing donated devices and distributing them for free to communities in need across the country, along with technology education for children and adults. Its classes can begin with how to turn on a laptop and extend through website building, workforce preparation and digital literacy, all with the goal of helping people become more economically stable.
Leisa Minor, Compudopt’s vice president of community partnerships, brought ideas from her TechSpark fellowship to not only help Compudopt streamline its own workflows but also to bring conversations about emerging technology directly to local families.
At the Douglasville AI Fair outside Atlanta in June, that meant making the learning a family activity. During the week before the event, Compudopt ran daily digital-literacy workshops for hundreds of children to prepare them for weekend coding projects at the fair, when parents joined in.
“The parents were blown away when they realized exactly what their kids were learning, and they were able to participate and build projects with those kids,” Minor says. “We were able to impact so many people at one time.”
Compudopt also has added AI exercises to its Pathways workforce program for ages 16 to 24. Participants work through practical career scenarios, including medical administration and elevator repair, using AI-generated research to consider possible solutions.
Earlier this year in Mecklenburg County, a room full of preschoolers sat enthralled, watching librarian assistant Traci Cruz — dressed up as a bear in a tutu and pearls — raise a dainty cup to her lips and pretend to sip tea across from a colleague in a mouse costume.
Little did the kids know their afternoon entertainment, “Madame Buttons and Squeaky’s Tea Party,” had been brought to them with the help of AI. The moment was another example of how local leaders are learning alongside residents about the potential of the technology.
Cruz, who runs children’s programming at the branch, had searched unsuccessfully for a two-person, age-appropriate, five-minute play she and a colleague could perform to kick off the summer reading program. She was desperate and “just wanted to punch the computer,” she says, until she remembered a technology she’d heard about but never used.
“It just came to me, why don’t you ask the AI?” Cruz recalls. She described what she wanted to a chatbot and watched it immediately “spit out” an idea. “I was just amazed. So now I’m like, what else can I use this for?”
Cruz is about to begin teaching classes about AI at her library branch.
She remembers one patron who used to call her over to help him watch boxing videos on a library computer. At first, he didn’t know how to click a mouse, but she showed him what to do and eventually watched in delight as he began finding videos and articles on his own.
“I think there’s a lack of awareness, that there’s something there that can help them,” Cruz says. “I’m hoping that as I show them the tool and explain to them how to use it, that it’ll make their lives better and more simple for them to do things that they’re having trouble with now.”
